Susanne M. Jaeggi* †‡ , Martin Buschkuehl* †‡ , John Jonides*, and Walter J. Perrig †

*Department of Psychology, University of Michigan, East Hall, 530 Church Street, Ann Arbor, MI 48109-1043; and † Department of Psychology, University of Bern, Muesmattstrasse 45, 3012 Bern, Switzerland

Edited by Edward E. Smith, Columbia University, New York, NY, and approved March 18, 2008 (received for review February 7, 2008)

Fluid intelligence ( Gf ) refers to the ability to reason and to solve new problems independently of previously acquired knowledge. Gf is critical for a wide variety of cognitive tasks, and it is considered one of the most important factors in learning. Moreover, Gf is closely related to professional and educational success, especially in complex and demanding environments. Although performance on tests of Gf can be improved through direct practice on the tests themselves, there is no evidence that training on any other regimen yields increased Gf in adults. Furthermore, there is a long history of research into cognitive training showing that, although performance on trained tasks can increase dramatically, transfer of this learning to other tasks remains poor. Here, we present evidence for transfer from training on a demanding working memory task to measures of Gf . This transfer results even though the trained task is entirely different from the intelligence test itself. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the extent of gain in intelligence critically depends on the amount of training: the more training, the more improvement in Gf . That is, the training effect is dosage-dependent. Thus, in contrast to many previous studies, weconclude that it is possible to improve Gf without practicing the testing tasks themselves, opening a wide range of applications.

F luid intelligence ( Gf ) is a complex human ability that allows us to adapt our thinking to a new cognitive problem or situation (1). Gf is critical for a wide variety of cognitive tasks (2), and it is considered one of the most important factors in learning. Moreover, Gf is closely related to professional and educational success (3-6), especially in complex and demanding environments (7). There is considerable agreement that Gf is robust against influences of education and socialization, and it is commonly seen as having a strong hereditary component (2, 8, 9). Gf can be compromised as seen in the effects of certain manipulations that threaten one's group membership (10). But can Gf be improved by any means?

In the domain of psychopharmacology, although there is a market for so-called ''smart drugs,'' there is no study showing evidence for a drug-related increase in Gf in healthy adults although there are certain psychomotor stimulants and D2 dopamine-receptor agonists that have effects on isolated cognitive processes (11, 12). Beyond the psychopharmacology, there is a growing interest in whether computer and video games may increase IQ. But in contrast to suggestive advertisements, there is no empirical evidence that computer games enhance anything beyond task-specific performance (13, 14) and selective visuospatial attention (15).

Of course, one can easily increase performance in tests of Gf by simply practicing the tests themselves (16). headline.statement: All three per-experiment comparisons of trained against untrained groups report a p-value roughly half the value their own F statistic and degrees of freedom produce, and once recomputed neither of the two called "statistically significant" clears the 0.05 the paper tests against.
headline.evidence: "revealed a trend for group differences after 12 days ( F (1,19) = 1.93; P = 0.09; ηp2 = 0.09), and statistically significant group differences after 17 ( F (1,13) = 4.65; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.26), and 19 training days ( F (1,12) = 4.53; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.27)". Recomputed from the printed F and df: F(1,19)=1.93 gives p = 0.1808 (reported 0.09; ratio 2.01); F(1,13)=4.65 gives p = 0.0504; F(1,12)=4.53 gives p = 0.0547. Halving all three gives 0.090, 0.025 and 0.027 -- exactly what the paper printed.
headline.plain: For each of its three training durations the paper compares the trained group against its untrained comparison group, and prints both a test statistic and a probability value. For all three, the probability printed is about half what that test statistic actually yields. Two of the three are described as showing a statistically significant difference; recomputed from the paper's own numbers they come out at 0.050 and 0.055, neither of which clears the 0.05 cutoff the paper itself uses. These two comparisons are the per-experiment evidence for the paper's second headline claim, that more training produces more gain.

findings.title: All three per-experiment ANCOVA p-values are approximately half the value their own F and degrees of freedom give
findings.reported: "revealed a trend for group differences after 12 days ( F (1,19) = 1.93; P = 0.09; ηp2 = 0.09), and statistically significant group differences after 17 ( F (1,13) = 4.65; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.26), and 19 training days ( F (1,12) = 4.53; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.27)"
findings.computed: recalc_f_to_p returns p = 0.180827 for F(1,19) = 1.93 (achievable interval over the F rounding 0.18029-0.18137, reported 0.09 outside it, verdict `suspicious`); p = 0.050365 for F(1,13) = 4.65 (interval 0.05026-0.05047); p = 0.054713 for F(1,12) = 4.53 (interval 0.05460-0.05483). The 12-day row pins the discrepancy factor at 0.180827 / 0.09 = 2.01. Halving the other two computed values gives 0.025 and 0.027, both of which would print as "P < 0.05".
findings.assumptions: The 12-day row needs no assumption: the paper prints an exact p and the tool flags it. The 17- and 19-day rows depend on reading the printed "<" as the strict bound the authors wrote. This must be stated plainly: recalc_f_to_p has no threshold argument, so it read "P < 0.05" as "P = 0.05" at two decimals and returned `consistent` for both of those rows, since 0.0504 and 0.0547 fall inside the interval [0.045, 0.055) that a two-decimal 0.05 asserts. On that reading they are ordinary rounding; on the reading the paper's own "<" asserts, they are over-claims. The halving account is an interpretation across three tool results, not a fourth computation. The innocent explanation is that the p-values were halved as though one-tailed -- routine for a directional t-test and a plausible slip if the authors converted from t -- but F has only an upper tail, so no one-tailed convention licenses it here.

consequence.explanation: The Discussion's dose-response argument cites "statistically significant group differences after 17 and 19 training days"; recomputed at 0.050 and 0.055 neither clears the paper's own 0.05, and the 12-day "trend" at a recomputed 0.18 would not ordinarily be described as one.

findings.plain: For each training duration the paper compares the trained group with its untrained comparison group, printing both a test statistic and a probability value. In all three comparisons the probability printed is about half what the test statistic beside it actually produces. The clearest case is the 12-day comparison, where the paper prints an exact value of 0.09 and the statistic gives 0.18 -- a factor of two, too large to be rounding. The other two are described as statistically significant; recomputed they come out at 0.050 and 0.055, so on the paper's own 0.05 standard neither quite qualifies. The most likely innocent cause is that the authors halved these values, which is a legitimate step for some tests but not for this one. It does not touch the paper's overall trained-versus-untrained comparison, which is much stronger, but it does weaken the specific evidence that longer training produced bigger gains.

findings.title: Degrees of freedom of the four training-curve regressions imply 68 trained participants against the 34 the paper analysed
findings.location: Results, footnote on the four training functions
findings.reported: "Note that the specific training gain was well explained by a linear function for all groups (8 days training: R 2 = 0.78, F (1,134) = 473.44, P < 0.001; 12 days training: R 2 = 0.81, F (1,202) = 863.59, P < 0.001; 17 days training: R 2 = 0.73, F (1,287) = 769.63; 19 days training: R 2 = 0.79, F (1,321) = 1230.23, P < 0.001)." Methods state 35 assigned to training, one excluded, "resulting in a final N of 34".
findings.computed: check_summation_batch, 5 rows, 1 inconsistent. Residual df + 2 gives 136, 204, 289 and 323 observations. Divided by the 8, 12, 17 and 19 sessions of each group these give exactly 17 participants in every one of the four groups (136 = 8 x 17 and 204 = 12 x 17 both reconcile at zero tolerance). Summing the four implied group sizes gives 68 against the 34 trained participants actually analysed: difference 34, verdict `suspicious`.
findings.assumptions: The modelling assumption is doing the work and is mine, not the paper's: this reads df2 as n_observations - 2, the residual df of a single-predictor linear regression, which is what "well explained by a linear function" most naturally describes and is consistent with the printed R-squared (R2 = F/(F+df2) reproduces all four printed values). It further assumes one observation per participant per session. Two innocent routes exist and neither closes the gap: two observations per session per participant would require exactly 8.5 participants in each of the four groups, which is impossible; and a regression fitted at block level rather than session level would give different totals again, but the paper does not say which was done. Because the finding rests on an assumed model rather than a stated one it is capped at `suspicious` and must not be read as an impossibility.

consequence.explanation: Bears on the Discussion's opening claim of "an impressive learning curve for the training task in all four experiments", which is fitted to roughly twice as many observations as the reported trained sample supplies under the standard reading of these degrees of freedom.

findings.plain: The paper reports four analyses showing that participants got better at the training task over successive days. Each analysis states how many data points it used, and working backwards from those, all four imply exactly 17 trained people per group -- 68 in total. The paper says 34 people completed training. Everything else about the participant counts adds up perfectly, which makes this stand out. There are ordinary explanations, most likely that the analyses counted something other than one measurement per person per day, but the paper does not say what was counted, so a reader cannot tell. This affects only the claim that people improved at the training task itself, not the claim that their reasoning scores improved.

findings.title: Two of the four significant primary results, including the interaction cited as confirming transfer, do not survive correction for their own family of tests
findings.location: Results, paragraphs 2-3 (seven primary transfer and dose-response tests on the same 69 participants)
findings.reported: No correction is stated for this family; Gabriel's procedure is applied only to the four post-hoc contrasts among training durations. The paper writes that the trained-group advantage "was confirmed by the significant group x test-session interaction ( F (1,67) = 5.27; P < 0.05)".
findings.computed: multiplicity_report over the seven primary tests at alpha = 0.05: family-wise error rate up to 30.2% if independent, about 0.4 false positives expected by chance. Of 4 results significant uncorrected, 2 survive under every method (Bonferroni, Holm, Benjamini-Hochberg and Benjamini-Yekutieli all give 2). n_claims_lost_to_correction = 2. The survivors are the trained-group pre-post gain (p = 3.9e-06) and the gain-by-training-time effect (p = 0.00017); the casualties are the control-group retest t (p = 0.0451) and the group x test-session interaction (p = 0.0248).
findings.assumptions: Family definition is a judgement I supply: these seven tests bear on one hypothesis in one pooled sample of 69 participants, which is the standard case for family-wise control. A reader who treats the four experiments as separate studies would define smaller families and lose fewer claims. The p-values passed are the exact values recomputed from the printed statistics, not the paper's thresholds -- six of the seven are printed as bounds and would otherwise be dropped, leaving the family uncheckable. Uncorrected testing was entirely ordinary in this literature in 2008; this is arithmetic about what the numbers imply, not an allegation, and the norm invoked is mine and not one this paper accepted.

consequence.explanation: The group x test-session interaction, which the paper explicitly cites as confirming that the trained groups' improvement exceeded the controls', is one of the two results that does not survive any of the four corrections.

findings.plain: The paper runs seven separate statistical tests on the same 69 people to support its two main claims, and does not adjust for the fact that running many tests makes a chance finding more likely. Adjusting for that, two of the four results it calls significant no longer are. The two that survive are strong and survive comfortably: the trained group's own before-and-after improvement, and the link between amount of training and size of gain. The one that does not survive is the direct trained-versus-untrained comparison the paper points to as confirming its central claim. Running tests without this adjustment was normal practice in 2008, so this is not a departure from the standards of the time -- it is a statement about what the numbers support.

findings.title: Two median-split analyses report an error degrees of freedom of 68 on a sample the paper elsewhere analyses with 67
findings.location: Results, paragraph 3 (median-split analyses of initial fluid intelligence)
findings.reported: "There was an effect of training ( F (1,68) = 6.38; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.09) irrespective of initial Gf as shown by dividing the sample into high and low performers in Gf at pretest (by median split). However, there was also a main effect of performance group ( F (1,68) = 4.56; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.07)". Elsewhere on the same sample: "F (1,67) = 5.27" and "F (1,67) = 14.08". Methods: 34 trained analysed plus 35 control.
findings.computed: No calculation: this is a cross-reference between degrees of freedom printed in two places and the sample size stated in Methods. 34 + 35 = 69 participants reconciles at zero tolerance (check_summation_batch, row 5, `consistent`), and 69 - 2 = 67 is the error df the paper uses for its other two-group comparisons on that sample. An error df of 68 corresponds to 70 participants -- the total before the one participant who failed to complete training was discarded. A two-factor between-subjects model on 69 participants would give 65, not 68.
findings.assumptions: The paper does not print its ANOVA model, so the reading depends on what design produced these two rows. One innocent route exists for the first row: a within-subject effect on 69 participants with no between-subjects factor legitimately gives an error df of 68. That route does not extend to the second row -- a between-subjects main effect of performance group on 69 people gives 67 under any standard model -- so the two rows cannot both come from a single coherent analysis of 69 participants. The likeliest benign explanation overall is that the excluded participant's pretest data was retained for these particular analyses; the paper does not say so.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this is a comparison between degrees of freedom printed in two places and the sample size stated in Methods, not an arithmetic result.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the two analyses supporting the secondary claim that the training benefit is independent of initial fluid intelligence; it does not bear on the transfer or dose-response claims.

findings.plain: Two analyses in the paper state a sample-size-related figure implying 70 participants, while the rest of the paper analyses 69 -- the one person who dropped out of training having been removed. The likeliest explanation is that this person's before-training data was kept for these two particular analyses, which would be defensible but is not mentioned. It affects only a secondary conclusion, that people who started with lower reasoning scores benefited as much as those who started higher.

findings.title: Every outcome value in the paper appears only as a bar in Figure 3; no table and no means or standard deviations are printed anywhere
findings.reported: "( a ) Mean values and corresponding standard errors of the fluid intelligence test scores for the control and the trained groups, collapsed over training time. ( b ) The gain scores (posttest minus pretest scores) of the intelligence improvement plotted for training group as a function of training time." The paper contains no tables; the extraction returned zero.
findings.computed: No calculation. This records what could not be reached: with group means, standard deviations and sample sizes, the fluid-intelligence score is a count of correct solutions in a fixed time, so it is integer-valued and the granularity checks (GRIM, GRIMMER) would apply directly; the two reported t statistics could be recomputed from the group statistics; and the two printed effect sizes could be tested against the values that produced them. None of that was possible. Only the weaker internal check was available, comparing each printed effect size against its own t and sample size, and the two are mutually coherent under a single standardiser.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. Values digitised from the bars would carry figure-derived provenance and are barred from the exact-arithmetic checks, so measuring the figure would not recover what is missing. Reporting outcomes graphically was and remains common in this literature; the norm that summary statistics should also be tabulated is one I supply, not one this paper accepted.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: this records that the paper prints its outcome data only in figures, which is a reading of the publication rather than a calculation.

consequence.explanation: The fluid-intelligence means, the gain scores and their dispersions -- the data behind every claim in the abstract -- cannot be checked at all, so the strongest verification tools available for this kind of study could not be pointed at the paper's principal result.

findings.plain: The paper never prints the actual before-and-after reasoning scores. They appear only as the heights of bars in a chart. That means the most powerful checks available -- the ones that test whether a reported average could have come from any real set of whole-number scores at that sample size -- cannot be run on the paper's main result at all. This is not evidence that anything is wrong; it is a statement that the central numbers are not in a form anyone can verify.

findings.title: Four null results are reported as bare bounds on a test statistic with no interval, so the effects they still permit cannot be stated
findings.reported: "There was no significant performance group by training-gain interaction ( F < 1)." "the gain in Gf was not dependent on initial working memory capacity as assessed either by pretest performance in a digit-span task ( F (1,68) < 0.3) or a reading-span task ( F (1,52) < 0.1". "but not on the reading span task, in which both groups improved equally in the posttest session."
findings.computed: No calculation was possible. The absence-of-evidence check requires a confidence interval, or a coefficient with its standard error; the paper prints only bounds on F, with no effect size, no interval, and in one case no degrees of freedom. Design sensitivity was computed where it could be: at 35 per group the smallest effect detectable with 80% power is d = 0.68, and within the individual experiments (roughly 9 per group) it is d = 1.45 -- so these nulls sit in a range where only large effects would have been detected.
findings.assumptions: None beyond the paper's own statements. "Not significant" is not "no effect", and the norm that a null claim should carry an interval or a sensitivity statement is one I supply; it was not standard practice in 2008. The paper is explicitly candid about one of these nulls, noting that "numerically the lowGf participants showed somewhat larger gains" and that it remains "cautious about this result".
findings.reproduction: No command applies: absence_of_evidence requires an interval or a coefficient with its standard error, and the paper prints neither for any of these four null claims.

consequence.explanation: These nulls support the Discussion claims that the training "proved to be useful for all participants and had no adverse effects for participants with high initial working memory capacity" and that the gain is unrelated to initial ability -- conclusions that cannot be evaluated without knowing what effects the data still permit.

findings.plain: Four times the paper says a comparison showed nothing, and each time it reports only that a number was small rather than reporting how large an effect the data would still be compatible with. With as few as nine people per group in the individual experiments, only very large effects would have been detectable, so "we found nothing" here is much weaker than it sounds. The authors are notably careful about one of these themselves, flagging that the lower-scoring participants did numerically gain more even though the comparison was not reliable.

findings.title: One of eleven partial eta-squared values does not match the F and degrees of freedom printed beside it
findings.location: Results, paragraph 3 (main effect of performance group)
findings.reported: "there was also a main effect of performance group ( F (1,68) = 4.56; P < 0.05; ηp2 = 0.07)"
findings.computed: The standard identity for a fixed effect, eta_p2 = F*df1/(F*df1 + df2), gives 4.56/(4.56 + 68) = 0.0628, which rounds to 0.06 rather than the printed 0.07. The same identity reproduces the printed value for all ten other partial eta-squared values in the paper, so the convention in use is established from the paper's own numbers rather than imported.
findings.assumptions: No registered tool converts F and degrees of freedom to partial eta-squared, so this arithmetic has no tool backing and the finding is recorded at `indeterminate` rather than as an accusation. The identity is stated in full so a reader can redo it. The obvious innocent explanation -- rounding 0.063 up to 0.07 by hand -- is trivial and consistent with everything else in the paper.
findings.reproduction: No command applies: no registered tool converts F and degrees of freedom to partial eta-squared. The identity eta_p2 = 4.56/(4.56+68) = 0.0628 can be checked by hand.

consequence.explanation: Affects only the printed magnitude of a secondary observation, that participants starting with lower scores gained more; no claim depends on it.

findings.plain: The paper prints eleven measures of how large each effect was. Ten of them follow exactly from the other numbers beside them; one is 0.07 where those numbers give 0.06. This is almost certainly a rounding slip made by hand and changes nothing, and is recorded only because ten out of eleven matching is what makes the eleventh visible.

triage.reason: Folded into the single ANCOVA-family finding (rank 1); the three rows are one defect with one explanation, and splitting them triples an accusation that has one cause. Quote re-located verbatim in the primary extraction, resolving the quote_not_located marker.

Same merge as the 17-day row; also re-ran recalc_f_to_p, which returns p = 0.054713 and, reading the printed 0.05 as a two-decimal value rather than a strict bound, calls the row `consistent` -- that tension is now stated inside the merged finding instead of being hidden.

Carried as the interpretation inside the rank-1 finding rather than as a standalone accusation, because the halving ratio was model-computed with no registered tool behind it; the three underlying p-values it rests on were each re-derived here with recalc_f_to_p.

Dropped from `suspicious` to `indeterminate`: no registered tool computes partial eta-squared from F and df, so the arithmetic is unaided, and the consequence is a rounding slip of 0.063 to 0.07 that changes no claim.
The omitted p-value computes to about 3e-83, far below any threshold the paper prints; a typesetting omission in a footnote with no bearing on any claim.

Preregistration and data-availability statements were not norms in this field in 2008; reporting their absence as a finding holds the paper to a standard its era never imposed, which is the error this stage most needs to avoid.

Kept at `suspicious` but rewritten after testing the innocent reading: a within-subject effect on 69 participants does legitimately give error df 68, which rescues the first of the two rows but not the between-subjects performance-group row, so the tension survives rather than dissolving.

not_checked.location: Figure 3a and 3b -- fluid intelligence means, gain scores and standard errors
not_checked.reason: The paper contains no tables and prints no means or standard deviations in the text; the extraction returned zero tables. The outcome data exist only as bars. Values read off the marks would carry figure-derived provenance, which is barred from the granularity and reconstruction checks, so digitising them would not restore what is missing. This blocks recalc_independent_t, rivets_independent_t, grim_check, grimmer_check and the internal-consistency form of check_effect_plausibility on the paper's principal result.

not_checked.location: Figure 2 -- mean n-back level per session for each training group
not_checked.reason: The per-session means underlying the four regression tests in the footnote appear only in this line plot, so the training functions cannot be refitted and the degrees-of-freedom anomaly could only be approached through the printed df, not through the data.

not_checked.location: Results, paragraph 2 -- Gabriel post-hoc contrasts (8 vs 17, 8 vs 19, 12 vs 19, 12 vs 17 days)
not_checked.reason: Reported as p-values alone with no test statistic, no degrees of freedom and no group means; nothing can be recomputed. multiplicity_report was deliberately not run on these because Gabriel's procedure already applies a correction and the paper says so, so adding a second would double-count.

not_checked.location: Results, paragraphs 3-5 -- the four null claims (F < 1, F(1,68) < 0.3, F(1,52) < 0.1, and 'both groups improved equally' on reading span)
not_checked.reason: absence_of_evidence requires a confidence interval or a coefficient with its standard error; the paper prints only bounds on F. The largest effect each null still permits therefore cannot be stated.

not_checked.location: Materials and Methods -- r = 0.95 correlation between speeded and non-speeded test versions
not_checked.reason: Quoted from reference 37 rather than measured in this study, and printed with no sample size and no interval. Only its logical bounds could be checked, and 0.95 lies inside them, which establishes nothing.

not_checked.location: Whole paper -- baseline comparability of trained and control groups
not_checked.reason: The Carlisle baseline-similarity family (csf_test, bayesian_table1_dispersion) was correctly not run: the paper reports no baseline characteristics table, only pooled age (25.6, SD 3.3) and sex (36 of 70 female) for the whole sample rather than by group, so there are no baseline p-values or group-wise rows to test. Allocation was also not randomised -- groups were matched -- so that family would not apply even if a table existed.

not_checked.location: Whole paper -- duplication checks within and across tables
not_checked.reason: detect_duplication requires two or more blocks of means and standard deviations. The paper reports none, so there is nothing to compare.
No supplementary files accompany this article in the supplied directory. This is 'not provided', not 'present but unreadable'.

not_checked.location: Results, paragraph 2 -- Cohen's d = 0.25 and d = 0.65 tested against the group statistics that produced them
not_checked.reason: check_effect_plausibility can test a printed effect size against the means, standard deviations and sample sizes behind it, which is the check that catches a mistyped value. Those group statistics appear only in Figure 3, so only the weaker consistency check against t and n was possible; the two printed values fall short of the paired-samples value by nearly the same factor (0.69 and 0.71), the signature of a legitimate alternative standardiser rather than an error.

not_checked.location: Design sensitivity for the omnibus and repeated-measures tests
not_checked.reason: required_n covers two-sample t, one-way ANOVA, correlation, chi-square and two-proportion designs. Minimum detectable effect was computed for the two-group comparisons (d = 0.68 at 35 per group; d = 1.45 at roughly 9 per group within the individual experiments) but not for the group-by-session interaction or the ANCOVAs, whose sensitivity depends on the pre-post correlation, which the paper does not report.

limitations: Figures were NOT read in this run. The figure-extraction pass was not invoked, and this agent reads text and does not see figures. Because this paper prints its outcome data only in Figures 2 and 3, that limitation is unusually costly here -- but note that even had the figures been read, values measured off bars carry figure-derived provenance and are barred from the granularity and reconstruction checks, so the principal result would still not have been verifiable.

The eight accusations from the numeric sweep all arrived carrying a 'quoted passage not located' marker. Every one of the eight spans was found verbatim in the primary text extraction during this review. The location failures are an artefact of this PDF: its page layer renders '=' and '<' as (cid:1) and (cid:2) glyphs, so the page-level and document-level extractions of the same sentence do not match each other. No finding was dropped on that basis, and none should be discounted for it.

This system reads one paper and reaches no network. It cannot say whether similar reporting patterns appear in other papers by these authors, and it cannot situate the reported effect against the subsequent literature on this intervention -- both of which a reader would need before drawing any conclusion from the findings above. That interpretation is partly ours and partly the reader's.

check_effect_plausibility holds no benchmark row for cognitive-training transfer effects, so the external-plausibility dimension was unavailable for this paper. The reported effect sizes were checked only for internal coherence against their own test statistics, not against any field benchmark.
The paper reports no tables at all, so tables_checked is empty. That is a property of the publication, not a gap in coverage of what exists.

The two most consequential findings each rest on a reading the paper does not settle: whether its printed 'P < 0.05' is a strict bound or a two-decimal rounding, and what the training-curve regressions treated as an observation. Both are stated inside the findings, and both are why confidence is medium rather than high.

questions_for_authors.question: For the 12-day analysis of covariance you report F(1,19) = 1.93 with P = 0.09. The upper-tail probability for that F statistic on those degrees of freedom is 0.181. Could you confirm which test produced the 0.09, or send the exact value your software returned?
questions_for_authors.why: Pins the one exact p-value in the family, where the discrepancy is a clean factor of 2.01 and cannot be rounding.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you send the exact p-values for the 17-day and 19-day analyses of covariance reported as F(1,13) = 4.65; P < 0.05 and F(1,12) = 4.53; P < 0.05? Recomputed from the printed statistics these are 0.0504 and 0.0547, both above the 0.05 the comparisons are described against.
questions_for_authors.why: Determines whether the two 'statistically significant group differences' underpinning the dose-response argument cleared the paper's own alpha.

questions_for_authors.question: For the four training-function regressions in the footnote, could you confirm the unit of observation and the number of data points in each? The residual degrees of freedom of 134, 202, 287 and 321 imply 136, 204, 289 and 323 observations, which at one observation per participant per session would mean 17 trained participants in each of the four groups against the 34 reported in total.
questions_for_authors.why: Resolves whether the regressions were fitted at session level, block level, or something else, which is the whole of the rank-2 finding.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you supply the pretest and posttest fluid-intelligence means, standard deviations and group sizes plotted in Figure 3a, and the gain scores and standard errors in Figure 3b? These values do not appear in the text and the article contains no tables.
questions_for_authors.why: Would make the paper's principal result checkable by the granularity and recomputation methods that could not be run at all.

questions_for_authors.question: The two median-split analyses in Results paragraph 3 are reported as F(1,68), while the other analyses of the same sample use F(1,67). Could you confirm how many participants entered those two analyses, and whether the participant excluded from the training data was retained for them?
questions_for_authors.why: An error degrees of freedom of 68 corresponds to 70 participants, the total before the documented exclusion; a one-line answer settles it.

input.report_markdown:
## What the paper claims

Four training experiments, pooled and analysed together: 70 young adults from the University of Bern community, 35 assigned to a demanding dual n-back working-memory task for 8, 12, 17 or 19 daily sessions (one excluded for non-completion, 34 analysed), each group matched to an untrained control group tested at the same intervals. Fluid intelligence was measured before and after with a 10-minute speeded matrices test, scored as the number of correct solutions. The paper concludes that training transfers to fluid intelligence, and that the size of the gain depends on the amount of training.

## What the design permits a review to reach, and what it does not

Two structural features condition everything below. First, allocation was not randomised -- groups were matched -- so the baseline-similarity family (the strongest instrument this system has for a two-group study, and the one that detects groups more alike than chance allows) does not apply. It was correctly not run. There is in any case no baseline table to test: age and sex are given once, pooled over the whole sample, not by group. A reader who wants to know whether the trained and control participants were comparable before training cannot find out here, and neither can this review.

Second, the paper contains no tables at all. Its outcome data -- the before-and-after fluid-intelligence scores and their dispersions -- exist only as bar heights in Figure 3. Since those scores are counts of correct solutions, they are integer-valued, which is exactly the case where the granularity checks are sharpest; with the group means, standard deviations and sample sizes, both reported t statistics and both reported effect sizes could have been reconstructed from first principles. None of that was possible. This is the single largest limit on the review, and it is worth being explicit that it cuts both ways: the paper's central claim was never exposed to the checks that would most strongly corroborate it either.

## What did verify

A good deal, and it is worth saying so plainly, because it is what makes the exceptions legible as exceptions. The participant flow reconciles exactly at zero tolerance -- 16 + 22 + 16 + 15 = 69 = 34 trained plus 35 control, after the single documented exclusion. Ten F and t statistics outside the three disputed analyses were individually re-converted and every one supports the significance threshold printed beside it; statcheck independently parsed three of the footnote regressions and returned no errors and no decision errors. All four training-curve regressions have an R-squared that follows exactly from their own F and degrees of freedom. Ten of the eleven partial eta-squared values reproduce from their test statistics. The two reported effect sizes fall short of the paired-samples value by nearly the same factor, 0.69 and 0.71, which is the signature of a legitimate alternative standardiser rather than a mistyped number, and implies an unremarkable pre-post correlation of about 0.75. This is what a carefully prepared paper looks like in the parts that can be inspected.

## How to weigh the exceptions

The discrepancies are not scattered. They are confined to one family of three tests, they share a single factor, and the one place the paper prints an exact rather than a thresholded p-value is the place the factor becomes visible. That concentration is what makes them interpretable rather than noise, and it is also what limits their reach: the paper's strongest results -- the trained group's own pre-post gain, and the relationship between training duration and gain -- are far from any threshold and survive every correction applied to them.

So the transfer claim is not overturned by anything here. What is weakened is the specific per-experiment evidence for dose-dependence, and the interaction term the paper cites as confirming that trained participants improved more than controls. A reader should also hold the degrees-of-freedom anomaly in the training-curve footnote separately from the rest: it is a real arithmetic tension, but it rests on an assumption about what those regressions counted that only the authors can settle, and it bears on whether participants improved at the trained task -- which nobody disputes -- rather than on whether that improvement transferred.

Several of the paper's reported values are internally coherent to a degree that argues against careless preparation. The pattern that remains is narrow, specific, and answerable by the authors from what they already hold.
